clinicalPearls: The commonest congenital cardiac anomaly, arising when two aortic cusps fail to separate, leaving a functionally two-leaflet valve that often carries a fibrous raphe
Frequently silent in early life but predisposes to accelerated leaflet calcification, so aortic stenosis or regurgitation tends to develop decades earlier than with a trileaflet valve
An ejection systolic click followed by a murmur in a younger adult should prompt evaluation for a bicuspid valve
Strongly associated with a bicuspid aortopathy: dilatation of the aortic root and ascending aorta that can progress independently of the valve lesion
Coexists with coarctation of the aorta, and any patient with coarctation should have the aortic valve assessed
Familial clustering is recognised, so echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives is often advised
Management centres on surveillance echocardiography of both valve function and aortic dimensions, with valve repair or replacement once stenosis or regurgitation becomes severe
reference.pathophysiology: A bicuspid aortic valve forms during valvulogenesis when adjacent cusps fail to separate, producing two functional leaflets that are frequently unequal in size and joined by a raphe. The abnormal geometry generates turbulent, eccentric flow and uneven mechanical stress across the leaflets, accelerating fibrosis and calcification so that stenosis or regurgitation typically appears earlier than with a normal trileaflet valve. The same genetic and developmental disturbance of the aortic wall matrix predisposes to dilatation of the root and ascending aorta, which can progress independently of valve dysfunction and carries a risk of aneurysm and dissection.
additionalDifferentials: Aortic root dilatation from Marfan or other connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to define leaflet morphology and quantify stenosis or regurgitation
Transoesophageal echocardiography for clearer leaflet and raphe definition when the anatomy is uncertain
Cardiac CT or MRI to measure the aortic root and ascending aorta and monitor progression
Exercise testing to clarify symptom status in apparently asymptomatic severe stenosis
Screening for coarctation and echocardiographic assessment of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Rapidly progressive aortic dilatation or a diameter approaching the surgical threshold, given the risk of dissection
Symptoms of severe aortic stenosis such as syncope, angina, or exertional breathlessness
Severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular dilatation or declining function
New murmur, fever, or embolic events suggesting infective endocarditis
Associated coarctation presenting with resistant hypertension
reference.prognosis: Many patients remain asymptomatic for decades, but the majority eventually require valve intervention, and the associated aortopathy adds a lifelong risk of aneurysm and dissection that mandates ongoing imaging surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing a young adult's aortic stenosis to degenerative disease and missing the bicuspid morphology
Monitoring the valve alone and neglecting serial imaging of the aortic root and ascending aorta
Failing to look for coexisting coarctation
Overlooking echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease
management: Regular transthoracic echocardiographic surveillance of leaflet function and aortic dimensions
Aortic valve intervention (surgical replacement or repair, or transcatheter replacement in selected patients) for severe symptomatic stenosis or regurgitation
Surgical replacement of the dilated aortic root or ascending aorta once it reaches the operative threshold to pre-empt dissection
Blood-pressure control and cardiovascular risk-factor management, with beta-blockers or angiotensin-receptor blockers to reduce aortic wall stress where aortopathy is present
Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI to monitor aneurysmal progression of the aorta
Screen for coexisting coarctation and offer echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives
Advise on endocarditis prevention through dental and oral hygiene, prompt evaluation of new symptoms, and cardiology referral for intervention timing
